title: X Feed Digest
summary: The dominant signal in this batch was that AI-agent infrastructure is getting real: crawling, tool-calling, shared context layers, and research-to-execution bridges are replacing one-shot prompt hacks.
AI coding discussion has also become more operational. The best posts were about long-task reliability, reproducible review loops, and context management—not flashy demos.

Model discourse is shifting from raw benchmark bragging to the settings that actually change output in production, like hidden reasoning defaults, quota policies, and how agents behave over long runs.

The clearest market call was Michael Burry’s bullish Hong Kong / Hang Seng Tech valuation case, while AI capital markets still look overheated through Cursor-style multiples and early infrastructure bets on agent payments.

The most useful general tactics were concrete learning and debugging systems: use NotebookLM to map a field quickly, and make agents prove bug fixes with a failing test before they touch production code.

items.title: @sitinme: Cloudflare Crawl Endpoint
items.body: Cloudflare’s new Crawl Endpoint turns full-site crawling into a single API call, handling JavaScript-heavy pages and incremental recrawls for you. That is a meaningful upgrade for RAG, search, and agent workflows because it removes a lot of brittle browser and anti-bot plumbing.

items.title: @OpenAIDevs: Responses API as Action Layer
items.body: OpenAI used the one-year mark of the Responses API to emphasize that the important shift is from chatting with models to letting them call tools, search, and run multi-step workflows. The signal here is that production AI stacks are increasingly being framed around actions and orchestration, not just text generation.

items.title: @kevinma_dev_zh: Trellis for Shared AI Coding Context
items.body: Trellis proposes a project-local context layer so tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex can share the same rules, task docs, and workflow state. If you bounce across multiple coding agents, this is a pragmatic way to reduce repeated prompting and keep standards portable across tools.

items.title: @SystematicPeter: NotebookLM Bridge into Claude Code
items.body: This notebooklm-py bridge treats NotebookLM as the research and extraction layer, then hands structured knowledge to Claude Code for execution. It is a sharp pattern for anyone doing serious reading-heavy work: separate knowledge digestion from agentic implementation instead of forcing one tool to do both badly.

items.title: @jarodise: Michael Burry’s Hong Kong Value Thesis
items.body: One of the best market posts in the batch flagged Burry’s latest argument that Hang Seng Tech is trading at an unusually deep disconnect between price and underlying business performance. Whether you agree or not, it is a concrete valuation thesis with a clear region and sector attached—not vague macro doomposting.

items.title: @TheGeorgePu: Cursor at $50B Shows Peak AI Froth
items.body: This post lays out Cursor’s valuation curve from $400M to $50B in roughly fifteen months and frames it against legacy industrial companies like Ford. The useful takeaway is not just the number—it is how aggressively the market is capitalizing application-layer AI winners despite obvious platform dependency risk.

items.title: @lyc_zh: Agent Payments Are Still Tiny, but Infra Is Moving
items.body: A good reality check on the agent-payments narrative: after stripping out wash-like activity, the actual volume looks closer to $1.6M than the headline numbers floating around. The reason it still matters is that Stripe, Cloudflare, Vercel, and Google appear to be aligning around the same payment rails before the market is large.

items.title: @dotey: Viral Amazon Layoff Thread Needed a Fact Check
items.body: This was one of the more useful news-hygiene posts: it argues a viral Amazon layoff thread mixed a real headline with unverified internal claims to manufacture panic. In a feed full of rumor-merchants, the meta-signal is to separate confirmed corporate disclosures from anonymous embellishment before treating any post as tradable information.

items.title: @yibie: NotebookLM Study Method for Fast Domain Mapping
items.body: A Stanford-style learning workflow stood out here: load textbooks, papers, and notes into NotebookLM, then ask for consensus models, fault lines, and unresolved debates instead of generic summaries. It is a much better recipe for getting oriented in a new field quickly because it builds a map of the territory, not just a recap.

items.title: @tangming2005: Fix Bugs by Reproducing Them First
items.body: A strong CLAUDE.md tweak: when reporting a bug, require the agent to first write a test that reproduces it, then let subagents attempt fixes and prove success with a passing test. This is one of those small workflow rules that can materially cut wasted agent thrash.

items.title: @chrysb: OpenClaw Cron Delivery Got Stricter
items.body: The OpenClaw 2026.3.11 release tightened cron-owned delivery behavior in isolated runs, which means jobs that relied on side-channel sending can now silently stop delivering. If you run automations, this is the kind of low-drama operational change that is worth catching early.

items.title: @wesbos: Paper Adds MCP-Native Design Workflows
items.body: Paper was pitched here as a Figma-like design tool with MCP support, letting agents pull from and write back to design state. The practical angle is that design tools are starting to become first-class participants in agent workflows instead of static handoff documents.
